extracted.intended_audience: scientists and educated readers interested in psychology, visual memory, and sensory phenomena
extracted.subtask_description: Observational classification and description of visual phenomena experienced by sane persons (visions, number-forms, synesthetic associations, phantasmagoria, hallucinations), plus methodological notes on collecting trustworthy cases. Also practical guidance on producing faithful telescopic lunar paintings using photographic aids.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence sourcing for cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Cases collected from four groups: personal friends of known accuracy; correspondents who wrote at length and whose letters bear internal marks of scrupulous truthfulness; material collected by many kind friends in many countries (each an independent center of inquiry); and brief replies by strangers to a circular of questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use diverse sources (personal acquaintances, detailed correspondents, decentralized collection by collaborators, and questionnaire replies) to assemble a large body of instances. Treat these as distinct groups and report their provenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-testing and verification of reports
rubrics_metrics.description: I have gone over all this matter with great care, and have cross-tested it in many ways ... I was soon convinced of its substantial trustworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before forming conclusions, carefully vet and cross-test reports for internal consistency and marks of truthfulness. Seek corroboration across independent sources to establish reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number forms (definition and characteristics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Number forms are an abiding mental peculiarity in a certain proportion of persons (say five per cent.), who are unable to think of any number without referring it to its own particular habitat in their mental field of view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterize number-forms by: lifelong presence (back as far as memory), constancy/unchangeability except gradual complexity, dependence upon verbal counting (angles/divisions at 'teens', twenties, etc.), and essentially mutually unintelligible diversity. Collect wire models or drawings if helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Color–sound associations (synesthetic associations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instant association of colour with sound characterizes a small percentage of adults (and is common in an ill-developed degree among children). The persistence of the colour association with sounds is fully as remarkable as that of the Number form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note that vowel-sounds chiefly evoke these associations; seers give minute descriptions of precise tint/hue and seldom agree with one another on which colour corresponds to a given sound. Compare collections and diagrams (e.g., letter/word–colour charts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Word–picture associations (visualized pictures tied to words)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain persons invariably connect visualized pictures with words — the same picture to the same word; printed words may have 'bad faces' or definite expressions tied to specific words or letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these pictures as regular concomitants of words, often traceable back into early memory. Collect sketches and first-person descriptions; use named informants (e.g., Mrs. Haweis) as examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dark-field automatic imagery (after-images, phosphenes, kaleidoscopic patterns)
rubrics_metrics.description: When in perfect darkness, many persons find a perpetual series of changes (kaleidoscopic patterns and forms) automatically occurring in the field of view — fugitive and elaborate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elicit reports by instructing subjects to watch their dark visual field closely. Compare experiences (e.g., Rev. George Henslow's vivid drawings) and note individual variability in vividness and controllability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual cycles and automatic chains of transformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Some seers experience a continuity of imagery where one image morphs into another (e.g., cross-bow → arrows → falling stars → snow → tulips → back toward the cross-bow), forming an automatic chain that can sometimes be guided back to a starting point by effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record sequences of successive transformations and attempts by subjects to exert volitional control; document partial successes and failures as evidence of interaction between automatic induction and will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between mental images and waking visions
rubrics_metrics.description: Mental images (voluntary visualization) differ from waking visions (involuntary) in voluntariness, suddenness, clearness, proximity, and duration. Images are under the will, formed comparatively slowly, fade slowly, and resemble a theatre back scene; waking visions are sudden, independent of will, extremely distinct (like daylight), appear/vanish instantly, and seem close.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When classifying a report, apply these criteria: voluntariness (can subject evoke/stop it?), suddenness (instant vs gradual), clarity (vague/shadowy vs distinctly impressed), and perceived spatial proximity. Use analogies (theatre back scene vs open daylight) to help witnesses differentiate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phantasmagoria (crowds of phantoms)
rubrics_metrics.description: A common form of vision is a phantasmagoria — appearance of a crowd of phantoms, sometimes in daylight but more often in darkness, often at the instant of putting out the candle or when preparing to sleep but not yet asleep.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record timing (e.g., candle-extinguishing, pre-sleep), typical phenomenology (crowd-like faces, never resembling acquaintances), and the subject's insight (usually not mistaken for reality). Note changes with health: when unwell the faces may come nearer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevalence of hallucinations among sane persons
rubrics_metrics.description: A notable proportion of sane persons have had actual hallucinations of sight, sound, or other senses at one or more periods of their lives; familiar hallucinations of the insane occur far more frequently among people in society and in normal health than commonly supposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting on prevalence, include a variety of social classes and note temporality (episodic occurrences). Collect anecdotal examples (authors, musicians' daughters, etc.) and contextual triggers (fatigue, slight fidgeting, not necessarily illness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity of visualization phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a continuity between all forms of visualization, beginning with almost no visualization and ending with complete hallucination; the continuity involves not only intensity but variations in the character of the process and multiple concurrent forms in the same person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider visualization phenomena on a spectrum; explicitly report co-occurrence of differing types in single subjects and document qualitative differences (channels of induction) rather than assuming a single-dimension intensity scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of photographic aid in telescopic lunar portraiture
rubrics_metrics.description: To paint a faithful telescopic portrait of the moon, Mr. Harrison first resorted to photographic aid: taking Rutherfurd's negative of the crescent, enlarging it by oxyhydrogen light, projecting the image onto canvas, and sketching outlines as the enlarged negative indistinctly presented them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use photograph-based enlargement to capture outlines, then consult the live telescopic image (lantern light in observatory) to sharpen details, mark intensely black shadows and high lights, and render gradations of tint. Combine photographic projection with repeated direct observation to improve accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observational-color constraints for lunar painting
rubrics_metrics.description: Accurately render phase-dependent lighting and subtle tints: the sun-illuminated edge may cast a yellowish tint over plains that gradates into grayish-green in the shadows; faint earth-light reveals outlines of features on the disk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When painting, note phase-specific color effects (sunlit yellowish tints, shadow gray-green, earthlight faintness) and represent terminator features (intensely black shadows, brilliant peaks, dazzling edge) carefully. Expect long durations (e.g., eighteen months to complete a phase) and limited sittings due to lunar phases and atmospheric conditions.
